articles.title: Self Citations in the Federal Judiciary
articles.content:
In the paper, we take a deep dive into decisions by the Federal Circuit and Eighth Circuit, looking at the extent to which judges cite their own prior decisions relative to citing those by other judges on the court. We also look at the rate that judges cite their own prior decisions relative to the rate at which they’re cited by other judges. Previous studies have used the rate at which judges cite their own opinion to draw conclusions about their individual behaviors relative to other judges, but to our knowledge no one has previously looked at this topic more broadly.
Our principal finding is that judges disproportionately cite to opinions they authored, but we were surprised by the extent of disproportionate self-citation. At the Federal Circuit, ten of the twelve studied judges cite themselves more than they cite any other judge, as do eleven of the twelve studied judges at the Eighth Circuit. For each judge, we compared self-citations to the number of citations to the third-party judge whom that judge cited most frequently, and the mean differences are a factor of 1.6 and 1.8, respectively. In addition, at both courts, every judge cites themselves more frequently than any other judge cites them. The mean differences are 1.7 and 2, respectively. The following graphs illustrate this for the set of Federal Circuit judges in our study.
The paper also develops a framework for thinking about why judges cite themselves. Dennis mentioned familiarity, which is a likely reason in many instances. But there may be motivations beyond that, including preferred language, doctrinal preference, marketing, and a desire to be consistent with one’s own past decisions. We also consider alternate explanations such clerk behavior and case selection effects, but conclude that they do not significantly explain the results.
If you’re interested in digging into this topic further, a draft of the paper is available on Iowa Research Online. Since the paper is still in draft state, we haven’t published the dataset yet, but are happy to provide it on request if you’re interested in replicating or looking more closely at our analysis.
articles.summary:
By Jason Rantanen and Jason Reinecke
Earlier this week, Dennis posted about the idea of self-citations by judges – that is, judges citing their own work – drawing on a  set of a Federal Circuit cases from 2021-2025 to show that this appears to be the case at the Federal Circuit.
Unbeknownst to him, we’ve been working on a full-legnth study of the extent to which judges engage in the practice of self-citations, a draft of which we’ve just posted to LawArchive.

articles.title: Clear but Absurd: The Federal Circuit Searches for a Middle Ground in Vicor v. ITC
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
Vicor Corp. v. ITC, No. 25-1616 (Fed. Cir. argued Nov. 3, 2026)
This is a follow-up to my post previewing the case. The case involves enforceability of a broad boilerplate patent license buried inside Foxconn purchase orders.
The briefing focuses on contract formation under UCC § 2-207 — whether a Vicor salesperson’s one-line email of ship dates accepted the purchase order and its license term. At oral argument though, Judge Dyk (sitting with Judges Lourie and Hughes) raised a different question: how much does the license actually cover?
General Term 10 of Foxconn’s purchase order says that the seller:
agrees to grant Buyer and its customer(s) a perpetual, irrevocable, non-transferable, and royalty-free license under all intellectual property rights included in the Products supplied to Buyer by Seller, so that Buyer and its customer(s) have the right to make, use, sell, offer to sell or import similar products or other products which contain the aforesaid intellectual property rights worldwide.
General Term 10. The plain reading of this seems to be that the seller (Vicor) is granting the buyer (Foxconn) and its customers rights to start reproducing the patented goods – even though this is just an order to purchase the goods themselves.
Judge Dyk saw the clause as ridiculously broad and suggested that the most sensible reading was as a license to replace the particular items sold under that purchase order, rather than a license to all of Vicor’s intellectual property for every future power module. When told that neither party suggested this reading before the ITC, Judge Dyk responded that the court has adopted intermediate positions between two extreme contract readings before. I don’t actually know what cases Judge Dyk is talking about, but I’m confident he’ll find them if needed.
The license terms appear quite clear on their face — and one way to think about this is what happens when a term is ridiculously broad. When asked about the clause’s meaning, Foxconn’s counsel, John O’Quinn (Kirkland), read the clause aloud at argument and noted that it reaches only the rights practiced by the purchased Vicor module. Nothing in that language limits the license to replacement units. Joelle Justus, arguing for the Commission, added that Massachusetts law does not permit a tribunal to revise a term to make it more reasonable.
I didn’t go digging deep here into Massachusetts contract law, but one interesting case is Berkal v. M. De Matteo Construction Co., 327 Mass. 329 (1951). De Matteo was building runways at Logan Airport. When its gravel subcontractor went bankrupt, De Matteo paid the subcontractor’s unpaid workers and suppliers directly and deducted those payments from what it owed. The SJC rejected the bankruptcy trustee’s argument that the payments were voluntary as contrary to common sense and good business practice, quoting an older rule for construing a contract:
So far as reasonably practicable [a contract] should be given a construction which will make it a rational business instrument and will effectuate what appears to have been the intention of the parties.
Berkal (quoting Bray v. Hickman, 263 Mass. 409 (1928)). Note the qualifier though – “so far as reasonably practicable.”
Of course, the panel may not need Judge Dyk’s reading – which would require substantial judicial redrafting of the agreement. In particular, there is a strong argument in this case that the purported acceptance email did not actually constitute acceptance. One struggle with this case is that these parties apparently had a course of dealing that included over 400 prior purchase orders, but the record says little about how those other transactions actually worked, beyond general testimony that these two orders were typical. (Vicor’s counsel pointed out that the license is Foxconn’s defense to prove.)

articles.title: Who Pays for the 500 Million COVID Doses? Section 1498 in Arbutus v. Moderna
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch

Arbutus Biopharma Corp. v. Moderna, Inc., No. 26-1581, oral args set for Nov 5 at the Federal Circuit.

You may recognize Moderna as key COVID vaccine developer/distributor.  Arbutus holds patents on lipid nanoparticle technology that Moderna used for its vaccine (without a license). The US govt bought about 500 million doses from Moderna that were distributed to the public.

The question on appeal is whether Moderna owes the money for infringement; or does the US govt under 28 U.S.C. § 1498(a).

Were the COVID-19 vaccine doses that the federal government bought from Moderna and gave to the public made "for the Government"?

If so, the Fed Govt takes responsibility for paying under Section 1498(a), and the case would need to be pursued in the Court of Federal Claims (CFC), with the United States as the defendant. If not, Moderna pays - something like $1.3 billion.

articles.title: Self-Citation in Federal Circuit Opinions
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch

Judges on the Federal Circuit cite their own prior opinions about twice as often as their colleagues cite those same opinions.

What I did here was analyze about 2000 FedCir opinions (2021-2026); extracted a list of their cited-authorities and then looked at the opinion author of the prior precedent.  The chart below shows the comparison -- Across the opinions, about 10% of the citations are to the opinion-author's own prior opinions.  This is about 2x the rate at which the rest of the court cites those same opinions.

The extra-cites are tied to opinion-authorship - not the panel.  Each appeal is heard by three judges, but typically only one writes the opinion.  When the two non-authors later cite that opinion, they do so at about the same rate as the rest of the court. Thus, a judge also cites opinions they wrote about twice as often as opinions for cases they heard but did not author.  One additional quirk here - A good percentage of the extra-cites are directed to a small number of opinions that a judge cites again and again.
